springBean.title: Spring IoC Container & 9-Stage Bean Lifecycle
springBean.subtitle: Visualize bean instantiation, Aware interfaces, BeanPostProcessor (before & after), @PostConstruct, and AOP proxy wrapping.
springBean.mentalModel: Spring beans pass through a 9-stage pipeline from definition scan to AOP proxy creation and singleton registry storage.

failureModes: Circular Dependency in Constructor Injection: Spring fails to instantiate beans when Bean A requires Bean B in constructor and vice-versa (resolved via @Lazy or setter injection).
AOP Proxy Bypass via Self-Invocation: Calling a @Transactional or @Async method internally via `this.method()` bypasses the BeanPostProcessor proxy shell, failing to start a transaction.
tradeOffs: JDK Dynamic Proxy vs CGLIB: JDK Dynamic Proxy creates proxies for interfaces (`Proxy.newProxyInstance`), while CGLIB creates subclass proxies by extending target concrete classes.
theoryData.productionScenario: An e-commerce order service had silently uncommitted transactions. Investigating revealed `orderService.processOrder()` was calling `this.saveAudit()` directly. Injecting the self-proxy or moving `@Transactional` to the entry point fixed the missing transaction boundaries.

interviewQA.q: At which stage of the Spring Bean lifecycle is AOP proxying created?
interviewQA.a: AOP proxying (CGLIB/JDK dynamic proxy) is created at Stage 7 during `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization()`. The container wraps the raw instance with a proxy that intercepts annotated methods.

quizData.question: Why does calling a `@Transactional` method from within the same class using `this.method()` fail to run in a transaction?
quizData.answer: Spring's `@Transactional` works via AOP proxies created during bean initialization. Calling `this.method()` invokes the target instance directly, completely bypassing the Spring proxy wrapper that manages the database transaction boundaries.

jpaEntity.title: JPA / Hibernate Entity Lifecycle & Automatic Dirty Checking
jpaEntity.subtitle: Visualize 4 Entity states (Transient, Managed, Detached, Removed), Persistence Context identity map, and automatic UPDATE SQL generation on transaction commit.
jpaEntity.mentalModel: Hibernate tracks managed entity field mutations inside the Persistence Context snapshot — when flush/commit occurs, it auto-generates SQL UPDATEs for modified fields.

failureModes: LazyInitializationException: Accessing a LAZY-loaded entity relationship outside an active Hibernate session (after EntityManager close).
N+1 Query Problem: Executing 1 query for parents and N separate queries for lazy children instead of using JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
tradeOffs: LAZY vs EAGER Fetching: LAZY prevents fetching unwanted related records but risks `LazyInitializationException` and N+1 queries. EAGER loads everything upfront but risks catastrophic join sizes.
theoryData.productionScenario: A reporting query fetching 1,000 customers generated 1,001 SQL queries and spiked database CPU to 99%. Replacing default `FetchType.LAZY` loops with `SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.orders` reduced execution to 1 SQL query, cutting latency from 3.2s to 12ms.

interviewQA.q: How does Hibernate Automatic Dirty Checking work?
interviewQA.a: When an entity is loaded into the Persistence Context (Managed state), Hibernate takes a baseline snapshot of its state. Upon transaction commit/flush, Hibernate compares the current state to the snapshot and generates SQL UPDATE statements for modified attributes.

quizData.question: What is the difference between `em.persist(entity)` and `em.merge(entity)`?
quizData.answer: `em.persist()` transitions a NEW (Transient) entity instance into MANAGED state. `em.merge()` takes a DETACHED entity, copies its state onto a managed instance in the persistence context, and returns the managed instance.

connectionPool.title: HikariCP Connection Pool Mechanics & Exhaustion
connectionPool.subtitle: Visualize thread connection borrowing, active connection leasing, pool boundary limits, and request thread waiting queues during load bursts.
connectionPool.mentalModel: HikariCP maintains pre-allocated DB connections in a pool; threads borrow connections for queries and return them immediately — pool exhaustion causes request queuing and timeouts.

failureModes: Connection Leak: Forgetting to close a connection or keeping long-running non-DB operations inside a transactional method holds the pooled connection hostage until pool exhaustion.
Pool Starvation: Configuring pool max-size lower than peak concurrent HTTP worker threads causes `SQLTransientConnectionException: Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms`.
tradeOffs: Fixed Pool Size vs Dynamic Sizing: HikariCP recommends a FIXED pool size (`maximumPoolSize == minimumIdle`) to eliminate latency spikes caused by on-demand connection creation.
theoryData.productionScenario: An API Gateway crashed under peak load with 30-second HTTP timeouts. Diagnostics showed HikariCP pool size was set to 10 connections for 200 Tomcat worker threads. Tuning pool size to `(CPU cores * 2) + effective_spindle_count` = 32 and setting `leakDetectionThreshold=2000ms` resolved the bottleneck.

interviewQA.q: Why is HikariCP significantly faster than legacy connection pools like C3P0 or DBCP?
interviewQA.a: HikariCP uses bytecode optimization, FastList (custom ArrayList replacement without range-checks), ConcurrentBag lock-free borrowing using ThreadLocal thread-level connection caching, and eliminates synchronized overhead.

quizData.question: What happens when all connections in a HikariCP pool are in use and a new request thread arrives?
quizData.answer: The new thread enters a FIFO waiting queue and blocks until an active connection is returned or until `connectionTimeout` (default 30s) expires, throwing `SQLTransientConnectionException`.
